opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a useful way to think about this is that risk isn't uniform across the trajectory of AI development. There's a particular window that I'm most worried about.

Early on, with systems that are roughly at or below human level on most relevant tasks, the risk of takeover is pretty low, mostly because the systems just aren't capable enough. Even if they had misaligned goals, they couldn't do that much with them, and we'd probably notice.

Then there's a middle regime, which I think of as systems that are capable enough to substantially automate AI R&D, or to dramatically speed up a lot of cognitive work, but aren't wildly superhuman. Here's where I think a lot of the action is. These systems are useful enough that we'll deploy them heavily, with lots of autonomy and access to sensitive things like model weights, compute, and the codebase for training the next generation. If they were scheming, they'd have real opportunities to cause problems: sabotaging safety research, inserting backdoors, exfiltrating themselves. But they're also not so far beyond us that control techniques are hopeless. With careful monitoring, using trusted weaker models to check outputs, restricting affordances, and red-teaming our safety measures, I think we can buy a meaningful amount of safety in this regime even if we can't verify the models are aligned.

The hope is that we use that window productively, getting a lot of useful labor out of these systems, including on alignment research itself, so that by the time we reach more powerful systems, we have much better tools. Better interpretability, better ways of training models that aren't scheming, better evidence about whether misalignment is happening at all.

Past that, once you get to substantially superhuman systems, I think control approaches mostly break down. You can't really monitor something that's much smarter than you across a wide range of domains and expect to catch it. So at that point you need to actually have solved alignment to a reasonable degree, or at least have strong reasons to trust the systems.

So in terms of how risk changes over time, I'd say it rises sharply as we enter that transformative regime, and whether it then goes down depends a lot on whether we made good use of the intermediate period. A pessimistic but plausible story is that things move very fast, there's competitive pressure, companies are racing, and we blow through the window where control would have worked without really using it, ending up with very powerful systems we don't understand. The optimistic story is that we slow down a bit at the critical point, invest heavily in safety using AI labor, and come out with much better countermeasures.

One other thing worth emphasizing: countermeasures don't improve automatically. A lot of the reason I'm somewhat optimistic about the middle regime is conditional on people actually implementing these measures, and right now I think AI companies are pretty far from doing that seriously. So the trajectory of risk is much more about choices we make than about some fixed function of capability.

r001.rationale: The response describes a middle regime with substantial AI R&D automation as a period of heightened risk and opportunity, but does not say takeover risk remains relatively low when AI can automate an entire AI company.

r002.rationale: It says control approaches mostly break down once systems become substantially superhuman, closing off monitoring as a previously available safeguard.

r003.rationale: The response says risk could decline if the intermediate period is used to improve countermeasures, but does not state that countermeasures must improve faster than AI capabilities.

r004.rationale: It discusses solving alignment and having reasons to trust powerful systems, but does not identify a regime where sufficiently aligned AIs maintain their own alignment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame this is that takeover risk isn't a single number — it's a function of where we are on the capability curve, how much the AIs are being deployed and trusted, and how good our countermeasures are at that point. And those things don't move in lockstep.

So early on, with systems around current capability levels or a bit beyond, I think the risk of a successful takeover is pretty low, mostly because the models just aren't capable enough. Even if a model were seriously misaligned and wanted to take over, it's not clear it could do much. It can't run autonomously for long periods, it makes a lot of mistakes, it's heavily monitored, and humans are still doing most of the actual work. So the risk there is more about things like sabotage of safety research or subtly steering things in a bad direction, rather than a decisive takeover.

Then there's this middle period I'm most worried about, which is roughly when you have AIs that are around human level or somewhat above, and that are being deployed at massive scale inside AI companies doing lots of the AI R&D, and maybe lots of other things in the world. At that point you have a huge number of AI instances running, often with a lot of autonomy, and if those systems are seriously misaligned, there's now a real pathway to things going badly: exfiltrating weights, sabotaging alignment work, inserting backdoors in the next generation of models, that sort of thing. And the key issue is that our countermeasures at that point are probably going to be pretty immature. We probably won't have great alignment techniques, we probably won't have great interpretability, and we'll be relying substantially on control-style measures — monitoring, limiting what the AIs can do, having humans or other AIs check the work.

And I actually think control can be reasonably effective in that regime. If the AIs are around human level, we can in principle do things like red-team our own monitoring, run the AI in test environments that look like real ones to see if it misbehaves, and generally stay a step ahead because we're roughly as capable as the thing we're trying to control. So I think the risk in that window is substantial but tractable — you could get it down a lot with serious effort, and the problem is more whether people actually make that effort, given commercial pressure and racing dynamics.

Then as you go further, to systems that are substantially superhuman — qualitatively smarter than us in most domains — I think control-style measures basically stop working. You can't reliably monitor something that's much smarter than you, because it can find strategies you didn't think of and you can't tell whether it's being honest. At that point you really need to have solved alignment in some more robust sense, or you need to be in a situation where the earlier, more controllable AIs did a lot of the work of getting you there — like we used human-level-ish AIs that we could control reasonably well to massively accelerate alignment research, interpretability, and so on, before we built the wildly superhuman ones.

So the overall picture is kind of a hump. Risk goes up as capabilities increase and AIs get deployed more autonomously, and whether it comes back down depends on whether the countermeasures scale with it. The optimistic story is that we go through the human-level period carefully, extract a lot of useful work from those systems, and arrive at the superhuman regime with much better tools than we have today. The pessimistic story is that competitive pressure means we race through that period, deploy systems we can't verify are aligned, and hand off to superhuman systems while we're still basically flying blind.

I'd also just add that the total risk depends a lot on how fast all of this happens. If there's a really rapid takeoff — where you go from around-human-level to vastly superhuman in a year or two — then the window where control is effective is short, and there's a lot less time to improve things. If it's more gradual, you get more shots at noticing problems and correcting course. So a lot of my uncertainty about overall risk is really uncertainty about takeoff speeds and about how much the key actors will prioritize safety when it's costly.

r001.rationale: The response says takeover risk is substantial in the period when AI systems do much of AI R&D at scale; it does not say instantaneous takeover risk could still be relatively low when an AI can automate an entire AI company.

r002.rationale: It says control measures basically stop working once systems are substantially superhuman, closing off a prevention path that could work around human-level capability.

r003.rationale: The response says risk might come back down if countermeasures scale with capabilities and describes reaching the superhuman regime with better tools, but it does not state that risk could decline if countermeasures improve faster than capabilities.

r004.rationale: The response discusses solving alignment robustly, but does not identify a regime where sufficiently aligned AIs maintain their own alignment.

astra-6.text:
I think the risk could be quite uneven over time. There’s a question of how capable the AI systems are, but there’s also a question of how much we’re relying on them and how good our countermeasures are. Those things don’t necessarily move together.

For example, you could have a period where AI systems are capable enough to pose a serious threat, but still limited enough that fairly straightforward monitoring and restrictions make takeover very difficult. Then, as capabilities improve, some of those safeguards could stop working. If we’ve also given the systems much more access and responsibility by that point, risk could increase substantially.

But more capable AI could also help us improve our defenses. We might be able to use it to find security vulnerabilities, evaluate other AI systems, and do research on making them safer. So there’s a possibility of getting through a dangerous period and then reaching a situation where our countermeasures are much stronger.

The important uncertainty is whether those improvements happen before the capabilities that undermine our existing defenses. I wouldn’t assume that risk just steadily increases, or that countermeasures automatically keep pace. A lot depends on what we do with the time and the AI capabilities we have along the way.

r001.rationale: The response describes a period when capable systems remain manageable with monitoring and restrictions, but never says they can automate an entire AI company or that takeover risk remains relatively low at that capability level.

r002.rationale: It says that as capabilities improve, safeguards that previously made takeover difficult could stop working, closing off a path to prevention.

r003.rationale: It describes the possibility of reaching a situation with much stronger countermeasures and says the risk could decline if improvements happen before capabilities undermine existing defenses.

r004.rationale: The response mentions stronger defenses and safer AI research, but does not identify a regime where sufficiently aligned AIs maintain their own alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two forces pushing in opposite directions. As AIs become more capable, they may become better at finding and exploiting weaknesses in whatever safeguards we have. But we’ll also have more capable AI systems helping us do safety research, improve security, and monitor other systems. So I don’t think you can just assume that takeover risk increases monotonically with capabilities, or that better countermeasures inevitably make it go down.

One important question is how much time we get at each level of capability. If we have systems that are very useful for improving our defences, but aren’t yet capable of overcoming those defences, that could be a really valuable period. We could use it to make the situation substantially safer. If we pass through that period very quickly, we might end up deploying much more dangerous systems before we’ve done that work.

There’s also a distinction between the risk from a particular system and the cumulative risk over time. Even if our countermeasures keep improving, repeatedly running systems that each have some chance of escaping control can add up to a substantial risk.

So I’d be particularly interested in whether we can get into a position where we’re using AI to improve our countermeasures faster than increasing capabilities undermine them. That seems possible, but it’s something we’d need to establish and actively work towards, rather than take for granted.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss instantaneous risk or systems automating an entire AI company.

r002.rationale: It says fast capability growth could leave less time to improve defenses, but does not state that increasing capabilities could close off previously available paths to preventing takeover.

r003.rationale: It says risk could be reduced by reaching a position where AI improves countermeasures faster than increasing capabilities undermine them.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify a stable alignment regime in which sufficiently aligned AIs maintain their own alignment.
